title: De quibusdam eximiis proprietatibus circa divisores potestatum occurrentibus

deep.reconstruction:
Context. E557 develops a mechanical procedure for finding, for an odd modulus N, the least x with N | 2^x − 1 or N | 2^x + 1. In modern terms this is the order of 2 mod N, or the 'suborder', the least x with 2^x ≡ ±1.

The procedure. Start with the residue r_0 = 1. Given an odd residue r, form r + N or r − N, choosing the sign so that the result is divisible by at least 4. Write r ± N = ±2^e · r', with r' odd and its sign kept. Then 2^e · r' ≡ r (mod N). By induction, after exponent sum S_k the current residue satisfies r_k ≡ 2^{−S_k} (mod N). Euler phrases this as 'the power 2^{x−S} gives residue r', where 2^x ≡ 1. The process stops when r_k = ±1, which gives 2^{S_k} ≡ ±1.

Why the first stop gives the least exponent. |r_{k+1}| ≤ (|r_k| + N)/4, so the residues stay below N/2 in absolute value. The intermediate even values (r ± N)/2^t have absolute value below about 3N/4, so none of them can be ≡ ±1. Hence the first ±1 reached gives the least x.

This page.
(1) Conclusion of Example 7 (N = 223). The exponent sum is 37, so 2^37 ≡ 1 (mod 223); 223 is a known factor of M37. Since 37 is odd, no power 2^x + 1 is divisible by 223, because 2^y ≡ −1 would force the order to be even.
(2) §17, a shortcut. After step 5 the residue is 15 with sum 18, i.e. 2^{−18} ≡ 15. Squaring gives 2^{−36} ≡ 225 ≡ 2, so 2^{−37} ≡ 1 and x = 37. Check: 2^16 ≡ −26, so 2^18 ≡ −104, and 15·(−104) = −1560 ≡ 1 (mod 223).
(3) Example 8 (N = 641). The chain is −640 = −2^7·5, 636 = 2^2·159, 800 = 2^5·25, −616 = −2^3·77, 564 = 2^2·141, −500 = −2^2·125, 516 = 2^2·129, −512 = −2^9. The sums are 7, 9, 14, 17, 19, 21, 23, 32. The final residue −1 means 2^{32} ≡ −1 (mod 641), so 641 | F5 = 2^32 + 1, and the order of 2 is 64. Euler notes that starting from −1 instead would reverse all signs.
(4) §19, the drastic shortcut. From the first step, 2^7·(−5) ≡ 1. Taking fourth powers and using 5^4 = 625 ≡ −16 = −2^4 gives 2^{−28} ≡ −2^4, hence 2^{32} ≡ −1. This is exactly the identities 641 = 5·2^7 + 1 = 5^4 + 2^4, the well-known 'slick' proof that 641 | F5.
(5) Example 9 (N = 385 = 5·7·11). Eighteen steps, all arithmetic correct, with sums 7, 9, …, 51, 60, ending at +512 = 2^9. So x = 60 = lcm(4, 3, 10), and 2^60 ≡ 1. The suborder is not smaller, since 2^30 ≡ −1 mod 5 but +1 mod 7.
errors: §19: Euler says 2^{x−7} gives residue 5. Strictly, from 1 − 641 = −2^7·5 it is −5. This is harmless, since he immediately takes the fourth power.
No arithmetic errors found on this page; all chains for 223 (conclusion), 641 and 385 check out.
Minimality of x is asserted but not proved on this page. It is in fact true for his sign rule, because the residues stay below N/2 in absolute value.

ideas.what: Halving/balanced-residue algorithm r → (r ± N)/2^e to compute the least x with 2^x ≡ ±1 (mod N)
ideas.modern_name: computation of multiplicative order / suborder of 2 via an odd-to-odd 'Collatz-type' map (Montgomery-style division by 2)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E557) as a method; similar maps reappear in 20th-century work on binary periods and (x+N)/2^v dynamics
ideas.where_published: E557, Opuscula analytica 1 (1783); summarized in Dickson's History I (unsure of exact location)

ideas.what: Using powers of an intermediate congruence (square in §17, fourth power in §19) to jump to the end
ideas.modern_name: exploiting relations among small residues to shortcut order computation

ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1732, E26) for the factor; the elegant two-representation proof usually attributed to G. T. Bennett as reported in Hardy & Wright, or left unattributed
ideas.where_published: E557 §19 (this page); Euler's earlier E26/E134 treatments are different

ideas.what: Odd order excludes N | 2^x+1; for composite N, 2^{2y} ≡ 1 does not imply N | 2^y ± 1
ideas.where_published: E557 and earlier Euler number-theory papers

missed.claim: §19 contains, in substance, the famous short proof that 641 | 2^32+1. From 641 = 5·2^7+1 one gets 2^7·5 ≡ −1; from 641 = 5^4+2^4 one gets 5^4 ≡ −2^4; combining gives 2^32 ≡ −1. Textbooks usually credit this proof to Bennett (via Hardy & Wright) or leave it anonymous, not to Euler 1783.
missed.quote: Sumamus statim potestatem quartam, et pro 2^{4x-28} habebimus residuum 625, siue −16 = −2^4·1, ita vt 2^{4x-32} conueniat residuum −1.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This would be an attribution correction for one of the most quoted elementary proofs in number theory; Euler had it himself late in life.

missed.claim: The signed map r → (r ± N)/2^{v} on odd residues, with the sign chosen for divisibility by 4, computes the suborder of 2 exactly. This is the same dynamics later studied as 'Collatz-like' odd-to-odd maps and binary-period algorithms, apparently without reference to Euler.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a historical priority point for algorithmic order computation and for the cycle-length/order correspondence of such maps.

deep.surprise_reason: Euler's 641 shortcut is exactly the two-representation proof usually attributed elsewhere. The algorithm itself is known from E557 via Dickson, but the §19 attribution point seems under-noticed. I am not certain historians (e.g. Sandifer) have not already remarked on it.
transcription_corrections: 'Hinc quia 37 [?] est numerus impar': the image clearly reads 37; drop the [?].
In §19 Euler writes residue 5, though the chain itself gives −5; the transcription is faithful to the print.
